title: Column and Row Manipulation, Deduplication and Validation

concepts.heading: Adding, Replacing, Renaming and Dropping Columns
concepts.body: Every DataFrame method returns a new DataFrame; the original never changes. `withColumn(name, expr)` adds a column or, when the name already exists, replaces that column, so `df.withColumn("price", F.col("price") * 2)` still has one `price` column. `withColumns({...})` (Spark 3.3) adds or replaces several columns from one dict. That matters in loops: calling `withColumn` 300 times stacks 300 projections in the plan, while one `withColumns` or `select` builds a single projection. `withColumnRenamed(old, new)` and the dict form `withColumnsRenamed` do nothing when the old name is missing, and `drop("a", "typo")` ignores names that are not in the schema, so neither call reports a typo. `select` with `alias`, or `selectExpr("price * qty AS total")`, projects only the columns you list, which is also how you reorder them. `filter` and `where` are aliases of each other and keep the rows for which the condition is true.

concepts.heading: Splitting Strings and Exploding Arrays
concepts.body: `F.split(str, pattern, limit=-1)` treats the pattern as a Java regular expression and returns an array. With `limit <= 0` the pattern is applied as often as possible; with `limit > 0` the array has at most that many entries and the last one holds everything after the last match, so `split("a-b-c-d", "-", 2)` returns `['a', 'b-c-d']`. Take one element with `getItem(i)`. `F.explode(col)` produces one row per array element (or per key and value of a map) and drops rows whose array is empty or NULL; `F.explode_outer` keeps them with a NULL value. `F.posexplode` adds a `pos` column next to the default `col`. A single `select` may hold only one generator such as `explode`, so to combine two arrays chain two `withColumn(..., F.explode(...))` steps, which yields every pairing of their elements. With ANSI mode on (the Spark 4 default), `element_at` raises an error for an index outside the array, while `try_element_at` returns NULL.

concepts.heading: Deduplication
concepts.body: `distinct()` removes rows that are identical in every column. `dropDuplicates(["id", "name"])` compares only the listed columns and keeps one row per combination; `drop_duplicates` is an alias. Every name in the subset must exist, otherwise Spark raises an `AnalysisException`, unlike `drop`. For duplicate detection NULLs count as equal, as in GROUP BY and DISTINCT where all NULLs fall into one bucket, so two rows `(2, NULL)` collapse into one even though `NULL = NULL` is not true in a filter. Values compare by exact characters, so `Ana@x.com`, `ana@x.com` and `ana@x.com ` stay three emails until you normalize with `F.lower(F.trim("email"))`. The docs do not say which duplicate survives; when it matters, for example the latest row per key, use `row_number()` over a window partitioned by the key and ordered by the timestamp, then keep row number 1. To list repeated keys use `groupBy("id").count().filter("count > 1")`.

concepts.heading: Validation: NULLs, Fill Values and Safe Casts
concepts.body: Validation separates good rows from bad ones without losing either. `dropna(how="any"|"all", thresh=n, subset=[...])` removes rows with NULL or NaN values: `how="all"` drops a row only when every listed column is empty, and `thresh` keeps rows with at least that many non-null values. `fillna(value, subset)` replaces NULLs but ignores columns whose type does not match the value, so a string default leaves an int column alone; a dict gives one default per column. A filter keeps only rows where the predicate is true, so `between(0, 120)` and its negation both drop a NULL age; add `isNull()` to the invalid set. With ANSI mode on, `cast("int")` on the text `abc` raises an error instead of returning NULL. To validate text, use `try_cast` (Spark 4.0), which returns NULL, and flag rows whose result is NULL although the input was not. `eqNullSafe` compares two columns and treats NULL as an ordinary value.

examPoints: withColumn with an existing name replaces that column; drop and withColumnRenamed ignore unknown names, but dropDuplicates with an unknown subset name fails.
explode drops empty and NULL arrays, explode_outer keeps them; only one generator is allowed per select; split with a positive limit keeps the rest in the last element.

distinct compares all columns, dropDuplicates(subset) only the listed ones, and both treat NULLs as equal; filters and their negations both lose NULL rows; under ANSI use try_cast to turn bad text into NULL.

quiz.q: A DataFrame `df` has the columns `id` and `tags` (array of strings) and the rows `(1, ['a','b'])`, `(2, [])` and `(3, NULL)`. How many rows does `df.select("id", F.explode_outer("tags").alias("tag")).count()` return?
choices: 3, because every id yields exactly one row no matter how many elements its array holds
4, because the empty and the NULL array each keep one row with a NULL tag
2, because only the rows whose array holds at least one element survive an explode of any kind
1, because explode_outer returns a single row that collects all elements of all arrays together
quiz.explain: explode_outer yields two rows for id 1 and one row each, with a NULL tag, for the empty array and the NULL array: 4 rows. Plain explode would return only the two rows of id 1.

quiz.q: `df` has the columns `id`, `name`, `ts` and the rows `(1,'a',10)`, `(1,'a',20)`, `(2,NULL,30)` and `(2,NULL,40)`. What do `df.distinct().count()` and `df.dropDuplicates(["id", "name"]).count()` return?
choices: 2 and 4, because the subset version keeps every row whose ts value differs
4 and 4, because rows containing a NULL in name are never treated as duplicates of each other
2 and 2, because distinct also ignores the ts column when it compares the rows
4 and 2, because the subset ignores ts and NULLs count as equal
quiz.explain: distinct compares all three columns, and no two rows are identical, so it returns 4. The subset id and name gives the groups (1,'a') and (2,NULL); NULLs count as equal in duplicate detection, so the result is 2.

recap: Column methods return new DataFrames: withColumn replaces by name, withColumns batches, drop and rename ignore missing names. split and explode reshape strings and arrays (explode_outer keeps empty ones). Deduplicate with distinct or dropDuplicates(subset), where NULLs are equal, and validate with dropna, fillna and try_cast, remembering that filters drop NULL rows.

title: Aggregations, Distinct Counts, Summary Statistics and Dates

concepts.heading: Counting, Averaging and Exact Distinct Counts
concepts.body: `df.count()` is an action that returns a Python int, while `df.groupBy("k").count()` is a transformation that returns a DataFrame with a `count` column. Inside `agg`, `F.count("*")` counts rows, and `F.count("x")` counts the rows where `x` is not NULL, because every aggregate function ignores NULL except `count(*)`. `F.count(expr)` counts non-NULL results of an expression, and a comparison such as `F.col("x") > 2` is false, not NULL, for a value of 1, so it is counted anyway; to count matches use `F.count(F.when(cond, 1))`. `F.mean` is an alias of `avg` and skips NULL, so 1, NULL, 3 give 2.0. `F.count_distinct(col)` skips NULL, so 1, 1, NULL, 2 give 2, while `distinct().count()` gives 3 because distinct keeps NULL as a value. With several columns it counts distinct combinations and skips a row if any listed column is NULL. With ANSI mode on, an integral overflow in `sum` raises an error; `try_sum` and `try_avg` return NULL instead.

concepts.heading: Approximate Counts, describe and summary
concepts.body: Exact distinct counts must shuffle every value, which is costly on billions of rows. `F.approx_count_distinct(col, rsd=0.05)` returns an estimate whose maximum relative standard deviation defaults to 0.05; a smaller `rsd` tightens the error at a higher cost, and the docs note that below 0.01 `count_distinct` is the more efficient choice. `df.describe(*cols)` returns count, mean, stddev, min and max for numeric and string columns, all of them when no names are given. `df.summary(*statistics)` returns count, mean, stddev, min, the approximate quartiles `25%`, `50%`, `75%` and max by default, and you choose the rows by name: `df.summary("count", "50%", "max")` returns exactly those three, and any approximate percentile such as `90%` is accepted. For named results use `df.agg(F.mean("x").alias("avg_x"), F.max("x"))`, or `groupBy("store").agg(F.count_distinct("customer").alias("customers"))` for one row per group.

concepts.heading: Epoch Seconds, Strings and Dates under ANSI
concepts.body: A moment has three forms: epoch seconds (a bigint counted from 1970-01-01 00:00:00 UTC), a date or timestamp, and a formatted string. `from_unixtime(sec, fmt)` returns a string rendered in the session time zone `spark.sql.session.timeZone`, so `1767225600` becomes `2026-01-01` in UTC but `2025-12-31` in a zone behind UTC; set the zone explicitly. `unix_timestamp(str, fmt)` parses a string into epoch seconds, and `timestamp_seconds(n)` turns seconds into a timestamp. `to_date(str, fmt)` parses a string, where the format describes the input text. In ANSI mode a numeric cannot be cast to a date, so `col("ts").cast("date")` on a bigint is rejected, and `to_date` or `to_timestamp` on text that does not match raises an error; `try_to_date` (4.0) and `try_to_timestamp` (3.5) return NULL instead. Pattern letters are case sensitive: `yyyy`, `MM` month, `dd`, `HH` hour 0-23, `hh` hour 1-12, `mm` minute, `ss`.

concepts.heading: Date Components and Date Arithmetic
concepts.body: `year`, `month`, `quarter`, `dayofmonth`, `hour` and similar functions return integers, and `F.extract` or `date_part` take the field name. `dayofweek` counts from 1 for Sunday to 7 for Saturday, so 2024-03-10, a Sunday, gives 1. `date_format(col, "yyyy-MM")` returns a string, `trunc(date, "month")` returns a date and `date_trunc("month", ts)` returns a timestamp; note the swapped argument order of the two. `datediff(end, start)` returns the days between two dates with the later date first, so `datediff("ship_date", "order_date")` is positive for orders shipped after they were placed. `add_months(d, n)` moves by whole months and clips to the last day of a shorter month, so 2024-01-31 plus one month is 2024-02-29. `last_day(d)` returns the month end and `months_between` the fractional month distance. Date columns hold no time zone; timestamps display in the session time zone.

examPoints: count(*) counts rows, count(col) skips NULL, count_distinct skips NULL while distinct().count() keeps it; mean is avg and ignores NULL.
approx_count_distinct has rsd 0.05 by default; summary("count", "50%", "max") picks statistics, describe picks columns.

from_unixtime gives a string in the session time zone, unix_timestamp gives epoch seconds; under ANSI a bigint cannot be cast to date and bad text raises unless you use try_to_date or try_to_timestamp.

quiz.q: `df` has a column `x` with the values 4, NULL, 4 and 10. What does `df.agg(F.count("*"), F.count("x"), F.count_distinct("x"), F.mean("x")).first()` return?
choices: (4, 3, 2, 6.0), because only count(*) keeps the NULL row and the mean divides by three values
(4, 4, 2, 4.5), because count(x) includes the NULL row and the mean divides by all four rows
(3, 3, 2, 6.0), because count(*) also skips the row whose x value is NULL
(4, 3, 3, 4.5), because count_distinct treats NULL as a third value and the mean divides by four
quiz.explain: count(*) counts 4 rows, count(x) skips the NULL and counts 3, count_distinct sees 4 and 10, which is 2, and the mean is (4 + 4 + 10) / 3 = 6.0 because aggregates ignore NULL.

quiz.q: A column `d` of type `date` holds 2024-01-31, a Wednesday. What does `df.select(F.datediff(F.lit("2024-03-01").cast("date"), F.col("d")).alias("n"), F.dayofweek("d").alias("w")).first()` return for `n` and `w`?
choices: n is -30 and w is 4, because the earlier date is the first argument of datediff
n is 29 and w is 3, because February is skipped and Wednesday is numbered from 1 for Monday
n is 30 and w is 4, because the end date comes first and Sunday is 1
n is 30 and w is 3, because Wednesday is the third weekday counted from Monday
quiz.explain: datediff(end, start) is positive here: 29 days to 2024-02-29 plus one more to 2024-03-01 is 30. dayofweek counts Sunday as 1, so Monday is 2, Tuesday 3 and Wednesday 4.

recap: Aggregates skip NULL except count(*); count_distinct is exact, approx_count_distinct trades accuracy through rsd, and describe or summary give quick statistics. Epoch seconds, timestamps and strings convert with from_unixtime, unix_timestamp, timestamp_seconds and to_date, and under ANSI mode bad text raises unless a try_ variant is used.

title: Joins, Set Operations and Broadcast Joins

concepts.heading: Join Basics: Keys, Types and Duplicates
concepts.body: `left.join(right, on, how)` defaults to `inner`. When `on` is a column name or a list of names, the names must exist on both sides, Spark performs an equi-join and keeps a single copy of each key column; when `on` is a Column expression such as `a.id == b.id`, both id columns stay in the result, and later references to `id` become ambiguous until you alias or drop one. The `how` values include `inner`, `left` / `left_outer`, `right`, `full` / `full_outer`, `cross`, `left_semi` and `left_anti`. Keys that are NULL never match, because `NULL = NULL` is not true; `eqNullSafe` lets NULLs pair up. Duplicate keys multiply rows: if two left rows and two right rows share a key, the result has four rows for it. Join on `["k1", "k2"]` to require all keys. Outer joins fill the missing side with NULLs, and a full outer join keeps unmatched rows from both sides.

concepts.heading: Semi, Anti and Cross Joins
concepts.body: `left_semi` is an existence filter: it returns the left rows that have at least one match, left columns only, each left row once however many matches exist, so it answers "customers with at least one order" without a later `dropDuplicates`. `left_anti` returns the left rows without a match; a left row with a NULL key has no match, so it appears in the result. Neither adds columns from the right side. A cross join pairs every left row with every right row: 1,000 rows and 50 rows give 50,000. `left.crossJoin(right)` states the intent. A `join` with no condition also produces the Cartesian product, because `spark.sql.crossJoin.enabled` is true by default since Spark 3.0, so a forgotten condition no longer fails loudly. Cartesian results grow multiplicatively, so an accidental one is a common cause of slow jobs and huge outputs.

concepts.heading: Union and Other Set Operations
concepts.body: `a.union(b)` appends the rows of `b` below `a` and keeps duplicates, so it behaves like SQL `UNION ALL`, and `unionAll` is the same method. Add `.distinct()` to get SQL `UNION`. Columns are matched by position, not by name, so two frames with the same columns in a different order are combined misaligned without any error; `a.unionByName(b)` matches by name, and `allowMissingColumns=True` (Spark 3.1) fills columns missing on one side with NULL. Other set operations follow SQL: `subtract` is `EXCEPT DISTINCT`, while `exceptAll` respects counts and also resolves columns by position; `intersect` removes duplicates and `intersectAll` keeps them. With `a` holding 1, 1, 2 and `b` holding 1, `a.subtract(b)` returns only 2, while `a.exceptAll(b)` returns 1 and 2, since one of the two 1 rows is cancelled.

concepts.heading: Broadcast Joins
concepts.body: A broadcast join copies the small side to every executor, so the large side is joined where it already is and is not shuffled. Spark plans it on its own when the estimated size of a side is at most `spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold` (10 MB by default, -1 disables); above that you ask for it with `big.join(F.broadcast(small), "k")`, `small.hint("broadcast")` or, in SQL, `/*+ BROADCAST(r) */`, where `BROADCASTJOIN` and `MAPJOIN` are synonyms. When hints conflict, `BROADCAST` wins over `MERGE`, then `SHUFFLE_HASH`, then `SHUFFLE_REPLICATE_NL`. With an equality key the strategy is a broadcast hash join; without one (a range condition) it is a broadcast nested loop join. Collecting the small side takes time: `spark.sql.broadcastTimeout` is 300 seconds. With Adaptive Query Execution on, a sort-merge join can also turn into a broadcast join at runtime when the real size turns out to be small. Do not confuse this with broadcast variables, which are the topic of day 10.

examPoints: Joining by name or list keeps one key column; NULL keys never match; left_semi returns left columns once per row, left_anti returns unmatched rows including NULL keys.
DataFrame union is UNION ALL and matches columns by position; use unionByName for names and distinct() for UNION; subtract removes duplicates, exceptAll respects counts.
Broadcast with F.broadcast, hint("broadcast") or a SQL hint; the 10 MB threshold and the 300 second timeout are the defaults; broadcast beats merge when hints conflict.

quiz.q: `a` has `id` values 1, 2, 2 and NULL. `b` has `id` values 2, NULL and 3. What does `a.join(b, "id", "left_semi").count()` return?
choices: 4, because a left_semi join returns every row of the left side
3, because the NULL row of the left side matches the NULL row of the right side
1, because each distinct matching key is returned once, however many left rows share it
2, because both left rows with id 2 match and NULL never matches NULL
quiz.explain: A semi join keeps each left row that has a match and never multiplies rows. Both rows with id 2 have a match in b, id 1 has none, and a NULL key matches nothing, so 2 rows come back.

quiz.q: `facts` is large. `dims` is the result of a filter, and the planner estimates 30 MB for it, so it plans a sort-merge join, although the developer knows only about 2 MB remain. The default threshold is unchanged. Which minimal change gets a broadcast join for this one join?
choices: Set spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold to -1 for the whole session, so Spark always broadcasts
Use facts.join(dims.hint("broadcast"), "k"), which asks for dims as the broadcast side
Replace the join with facts.crossJoin(dims) and filter the matching keys afterwards
Call dims.repartition(200) first, so that every executor receives a part of dims
quiz.explain: A broadcast hint (or F.broadcast) requests the broadcast regardless of the size estimate. A threshold of -1 disables automatic broadcasting, a cross join is far more expensive, and repartitioning dims causes a shuffle rather than a broadcast.

recap: Pick the join type by the result you need: inner, outer, semi for existence, anti for absence, cross only on purpose. NULL keys never match and duplicate keys multiply rows. DataFrame union is UNION ALL by position. Broadcast joins avoid shuffling the large side, are planned under 10 MB or requested by a hint, and use a nested loop without an equality key.

title: Schemas on Read and Write, Sorting, Printing and Converting to Lists

concepts.heading: Reading with an Explicit Schema
concepts.body: `spark.read.schema("id INT, name STRING")` accepts a DDL string or a `StructType`. An explicit schema avoids the extra pass over the data that `inferSchema` needs for CSV, and it fixes the types: inference turns a zip such as `00742` into the number 742, so declare identifiers as `STRING`. For CSV, `header` defaults to false, so with a header line add `option("header", True)`; without it the header becomes a data row, and a value that cannot be parsed as `INT` turns into NULL. The schema is applied by position: with the default `enforceSchema=true` the header names are ignored, so the fields must be declared in the file's column order, and a mismatched order leaves wrong values in the wrong columns without any error. Set `enforceSchema` to false to have Spark check the header against the schema. Parquet and ORC files carry their own schema, so `inferSchema` has no effect on them; Parquet columns are read as nullable.

concepts.heading: Malformed Records and JSON Layout
concepts.body: The `mode` option of the CSV and JSON readers controls what happens to a record that cannot be parsed. `PERMISSIVE` is the default: the bad fields become NULL, and if the schema contains a string column named `_corrupt_record` (or the name set with `columnNameOfCorruptRecord`) the raw text is stored there. `DROPMALFORMED` silently drops the bad rows, and `FAILFAST` raises an exception at the first one, which is the right choice when a nightly job must not hide bad input. Because reads are lazy, the failure appears when an action runs, not on the `read` line. JSON files are read as JSON Lines by default: every line is one complete object. A pretty-printed file, or one array spread over many lines, needs `option("multiLine", True)`; otherwise the DataFrame consists of a single `_corrupt_record` column. `samplingRatio` limits how many JSON objects or CSV rows schema inference reads.

concepts.heading: Schemas on Write and in the DataFrame
concepts.body: `df.schema` is a `StructType`, `df.dtypes` lists name and type pairs, `df.columns` the names, and `df.printSchema()` prints the tree, with `level` limiting the depth of nested fields. A list of Python tuples becomes `long` for an int, `string` for text and `array<string>` for a list, with `element` and `containsNull = true` shown for arrays, and inferred fields are nullable. Output formats differ: CSV stores neither names nor types, so a round trip without `header` on write and read gives `_c0`, `_c1` of type string, whereas Parquet and ORC preserve the schema. To change types before a write, cast the columns; under ANSI mode a `cast` or an insert into a table with a narrower type, for example a bigint that does not fit an int column, raises an overflow error, and `try_cast` returns NULL instead. Inserts into tables also follow `spark.sql.storeAssignmentPolicy`, which defaults to ANSI.

concepts.heading: Sorting, Iterating and Converting to Lists
concepts.body: `orderBy` and `sort` produce a global order, which needs a shuffle; `sortWithinPartitions` sorts each partition only, which is enough when every output file must be ordered. Mixed directions use `orderBy("dept", F.desc("salary"))`. Ascending order puts NULL first and descending puts NULL last by default; `asc_nulls_last()` and the related methods change that. `collect()` returns a list of `Row` objects on the driver, read as `rows[1]["v"]` or `rows[1].v`; `take(n)` and `head(n)` return a list, `limit(n)` returns a DataFrame. `toPandas()` and `collect()` load all rows into driver memory. `toLocalIterator()` streams the rows to the driver and needs memory for about the largest partition. `foreach` and `foreachPartition` run on the executors, so printing inside them does not show on the driver. `isEmpty()` is the cheap test for "any rows", better than `count() == 0`.

examPoints: A CSV schema is positional and header must be set explicitly; read identifiers as STRING; Parquet is self-describing and ignores inferSchema.
PERMISSIVE nulls bad fields, DROPMALFORMED drops rows, FAILFAST raises; pretty-printed JSON needs multiLine; failures surface at the action.
orderBy is a global sort, sortWithinPartitions is not; ascending puts NULL first; collect and toPandas need all data on the driver, toLocalIterator one partition at a time.

quiz.q: A CSV file has the header `id,qty` and the rows `1,5` and `2,oops`. The code `rows = spark.read.schema("id INT, qty INT").option("header", True).csv(path).collect()` runs with no `mode` option. What does `rows` contain?
choices: An exception, because the text oops cannot be converted to INT in any read mode
One row, `(1, 5)`, because malformed rows are dropped by default
Two rows, `(1, 5)` and `(2, None)`, because PERMISSIVE nulls the bad field
Three rows, because the header line is also kept as a data row when a schema is given
quiz.explain: The default mode is PERMISSIVE: the unparsable qty becomes NULL and the row stays. Dropping rows needs DROPMALFORMED, failing needs FAILFAST, and header is set, so the header line is not data.

quiz.q: `df` has a column `score` with the values 10, NULL and 30. What does `[r.score for r in df.orderBy("score").collect()]` return?
choices: [None, 10, 30], because ascending order places NULL first by default
[10, 30, None], because NULL is always the largest value in an ascending sort
[30, 10, None], because orderBy without a direction sorts from high to low
[10, None, 30], because orderBy keeps rows with a NULL key at their original position
quiz.explain: orderBy sorts ascending unless told otherwise, and ascending order puts NULL first. To move NULL to the end use asc_nulls_last().

recap: Read with an explicit schema, in file order for CSV, with header set and identifiers as strings; mode decides how bad records are handled, and JSON needs multiLine for pretty-printed files. printSchema, dtypes and schema describe the frame. Sort globally with orderBy, per partition with sortWithinPartitions, and bring data to the driver with collect, toLocalIterator or toPandas only when it fits.

title: UDFs, Stateful Operators, Broadcast Variables and Accumulators

concepts.heading: Python UDFs: Types, NULLs and Determinism
concepts.body: A UDF wraps a Python function so that it can run on column values: `F.udf(lambda s: ..., "int")`. The return type defaults to `StringType` when omitted, and `spark.udf.register("name", f, returnType)` makes it callable from SQL with the same default. The function receives `None` for a NULL, so `s.upper()` on a NULL fails the task with an exception in the worker; handle `None` inside the function. Spark does not short-circuit UDF calls: wrapping the call in `F.when(cond, udf(...))` or an `AND` does not stop it from running on the rows that fail the condition, so put the check inside the function. A UDF is assumed deterministic, which allows the optimizer to merge or repeat calls; call `asNondeterministic()` for random or time-dependent logic. The Catalyst optimizer cannot look inside a UDF, so prefer a built-in function from `pyspark.sql.functions` when one exists. Vectorized pandas UDFs process batches and are covered on day 16.

concepts.heading: Stateful Operators in Python
concepts.body: Stateful streaming code keeps data per key from one micro-batch to the next, for example a session record per user. `groupBy("user_id").applyInPandasWithState(func, outputStructType, stateStructType, outputMode, timeoutConf)` (Spark 3.4, Spark Connect from 3.5) calls `func(key, Iterator[pandas.DataFrame], state)` and expects an `Iterator[pandas.DataFrame]` back; `state` is a `GroupState` that the function reads and updates, and timeouts call it again with empty input. Since Spark 4.0 the docs encourage the new `transformWithState` operator over the legacy `mapGroupsWithState` and `flatMapGroupsWithState`. Its Python form is `transformWithStateInPandas(statefulProcessor, outputStructType, outputMode, timeMode)`. The processor is a `StatefulProcessor` subclass: `init(self, handle)` declares state variables, for example `handle.getValueState("numViolations", schema)`, `handleInputRows(self, key, rows)` processes the rows of one key and yields pandas DataFrames, and `close()` cleans up. Plain object attributes are not durable state. Both operators need a full shuffle by the key.

concepts.heading: StateStores and RocksDB
concepts.body: The state of a stateful query lives in a StateStore on the executors and is saved to the checkpoint location after each batch, so a restarted query continues from its state. The default provider keeps all state in an in-memory map inside the executor JVM and backs it with files in a checkpoint file system. With millions of keys this produces large JVM garbage-collection pauses and uneven micro-batch times. Since Spark 3.2 a RocksDB provider keeps state in native memory and local disk instead; switch with `spark.conf.set("spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.providerClass", "org.apache.spark.sql.execution.streaming.state.RocksDBStateStoreProvider")` before the query starts. It serves streaming aggregations, `dropDuplicates`, stream-stream joins and the arbitrary stateful operators alike. Changelog checkpointing (`spark.sql.streaming.stateStore.rocksdb.changelogCheckpointing.enabled`, off by default) uploads small change logs instead of full snapshots at commit. Watermarks bound how long state is kept, so state without a watermark can grow without limit.

concepts.heading: Broadcast Variables and Accumulators
concepts.body: Spark has two shared-variable types besides ordinary closures. A broadcast variable, `bc = spark.sparkContext.broadcast(codes)`, caches a read-only value on each executor instead of shipping it with every task; tasks read `bc.value`, and the driver must not change the object afterwards. `bc.unpersist()` frees the executor copies and a later use re-broadcasts, while `bc.destroy()` is final. An accumulator, `acc = sc.accumulator(0)`, is the opposite direction: tasks can only add to it with an associative, commutative operation, and only the driver reads `acc.value`. Updates are lazy: nothing is added until an action runs the code. Inside an action such as `foreach` Spark applies each task's update once; inside a transformation, or a UDF in `withColumn`, updates can be applied again when tasks or stages are re-executed, so the total may be too high. A Python global changed inside a task changes only the executor's own copy, and the driver still sees `0`. `SparkContext` is not available in Spark Connect.

examPoints: A Python UDF returns string unless a type is given, receives None for NULL, is not short-circuited by when or AND, and is deterministic unless marked asNondeterministic.
applyInPandasWithState takes (key, Iterator[pdf], state); transformWithStateInPandas declares state in init via the handle; large keyed state with GC pauses points to the RocksDB provider.
Broadcast variable: read-only, driver to tasks, unpersist or destroy. Accumulator: add-only, only the driver reads it, exactly once only for updates inside actions.

quiz.q: After the code `acc = sc.accumulator(0)`, then `sc.parallelize(range(4), 2).foreach(lambda x: acc.add(x))` runs on a cluster, what does `print(acc.value)` show on the driver?
choices: 0, because executor updates stay on the executors until collect() brings them back
6, because foreach is an action, so each task's update is applied once
12, because each of the two partitions adds the complete sum of the range
An error, because an accumulator cannot be updated from inside a lambda function
quiz.explain: foreach is an action, so the tasks add 0+1+2+3 = 6 and the driver reads the total. Accumulator updates need no collect call, and a lambda that calls add is allowed.

quiz.q: A UDF checks every value against a Python dict of 200,000 entries that it reads from a driver variable, and shipping the dict with each task is slow. Which change fits the Spark shared-variable model?
choices: Store the dict in an accumulator and let the UDF read acc.value for each row
Convert the dict to a global variable that each task updates for the executors
Create bc = spark.sparkContext.broadcast(d) and read bc.value inside the UDF
Call asNondeterministic() on the UDF, so Spark keeps the dict on each executor
quiz.explain: A broadcast variable caches a read-only value once per executor. Tasks cannot read an accumulator, a global changed in a task affects only that executor's copy, and determinism has no effect on how data is shipped.

recap: Python UDFs default to string, see None for NULL, are not short-circuited and are assumed deterministic. Stateful streaming code keeps per-key state in a StateStore: applyInPandasWithState and transformWithStateInPandas are the Python entry points, and RocksDB helps with millions of keys. Broadcast variables send read-only data to tasks, accumulators send add-only counts back to the driver.
